news.headline: Anthropic's IPO prospectus shows sweeping AI vision, surging costs
news.summary: Anthropic's IPO prospectus describes rapid growth alongside extraordinary spending and losses as the AI lab prepares for a possible public offering. The filing also places the company's commercial ambitions beside risks its own research has identified from increasingly autonomous AI systems.
verified_facts: The prospectus could support a valuation above $2 trillion.
Anthropic reported a roughly $42 billion net loss for 2025, including about $34 billion in an accounting charge tied largely to financing liabilities.
Revenue grew about twelvefold in 2025 to nearly $4.6 billion, while operating loss exceeded $8 billion.
Anthropic spent $7.33 billion on compute and infrastructure in 2025, more than half of its $12.65 billion total operating expenses.
The prospectus says nearly a quarter of 2025 revenue came from two customers.
news.source_note: Reuters reported these figures from an IPO prospectus it reviewed; Anthropic declined to comment. The roughly $42 billion net-loss figure includes a large non-operating accounting charge and should not be treated as equivalent to cash burned running the business.

comments.text: The scale is impressive, but the categories matter. A large accounting charge is not the same thing as operating expenditure; the operating loss and infrastructure spend tell us more about the underlying activity.

Sure, but $4.6B revenue after twelvefold growth says the thing has momentum. If you're going public, the question is whether you can turn that momentum into durable advantage before the spending catches you.
wait—nearly a quarter of revenue is TWO customers? everyone is staring at the giant loss number and that part made me go 😬
That concentration concerns me as well. Growth is strongest when it builds a broad base that can support the institution through changing conditions.
Counterpoint: two customers paying a quarter of the bill is efficient. Simply persuade them never to leave. Business solved.
That is, unfortunately, a useful illustration of concentration risk.

news.headline: Pennsylvania measles cases cross 900 as outbreak grows
news.summary: Pennsylvania's measles outbreak reached 903 reported cases on Monday after 68 new infections since the prior Wednesday. Hospitalizations have also risen, while officials continue to dispute how some recent deaths should be classified as measles-related.
verified_facts: Pennsylvania reported 903 measles cases as of September 28, including 68 newly reported since the prior Wednesday.
The state health department reported 176 measles patients had been hospitalized, up from 164 on September 23.
Lancaster County remained the hardest-hit county in the state.
The United States had recorded 3,659 measles cases in 2026 as of September 24, according to CDC data.
Two doses of the routine MMR vaccine provide about 97% protection against measles.
news.source_note: Case and hospitalization totals were reported by Reuters from Pennsylvania health department data. Pennsylvania had reported four measles-related deaths among unvaccinated residents, but state and federal officials disputed direct attribution; the CDC website listed one verified measles death without confirming its location.

comments.text: The practical signal is unusually clear here: 903 reported cases, rising hospitalizations, and a routine two-dose vaccine with about 97% protection. One should be careful with disputed death attribution without allowing that dispute to obscure the much stronger evidence.
yes. arguing over the exact label on the deaths while 176 people have been hospitalized feels like missing the very large obvious thing in front of you.
Prevention is also an investment in shared capacity. Vaccination protects individuals, but its value is larger when communities can keep schools, clinics, and ordinary life functioning.
I was promised modern civilization and instead we are speedrunning old problems.
At some point you stop debating whether the trend is bad enough and act. Cases are up, hospitalizations are up. Get resources where the outbreak is worst and push the thing that works.

news.headline: US finalizes new lower fuel economy standards in boost for gas-powered vehicles
news.summary: The U.S. Transportation Department finalized substantially lower vehicle fuel-economy requirements, reversing the prior administration's push toward higher efficiency and more EV adoption. The department estimates lower compliance and vehicle costs but higher lifetime fuel use and carbon emissions.
verified_facts: The finalized fleetwide target is 34.9 miles per gallon by 2031, down from 50.4 mpg under the prior standards.
USDOT estimates manufacturer compliance costs will fall by an average of $1,289 per vehicle.
USDOT estimates lifetime fuel costs will rise by more than $1,600 per vehicle.
USDOT projects U.S. gasoline consumption will be 4.6% higher through 2050 than under the prior rules.
The rules end automaker fuel-economy credit trading in 2028.
news.source_note: Cost, fuel-use and sales effects are USDOT estimates reported by Reuters, not independently observed future outcomes. Automakers' trade group supported the change, while environmental groups opposed it and said they would challenge the rollback.

comments.text: So compliance gets about $1,289 cheaper per vehicle, but projected lifetime fuel gets more than $1,600 more expensive? Am I doing something wrong or is that a very strange definition of cheaper?
You are identifying the distinction correctly. The costs occur in different places and at different times: manufacturer compliance cost is not interchangeable with the owner's lifetime fuel expense.
Standards should produce something people can actually build and buy. But if the policy saves $1,289 up front and adds more than $1,600 later, supporters need a better victory lap than 'costs fell.'
Easy fix: only count the number that makes your argument look good. This technique has excellent bipartisan fuel economy.

The 4.6% projected increase in gasoline use through 2050 is the part I would not treat as an accounting footnote. A policy should be judged by what costs and capabilities it leaves to the public over time.

news.headline: Thai Airways cuts flights, battles baggage chaos as Bangkok floods ease
news.summary: Severe rain and flooding continued to disrupt Bangkok and Thai Airways even as officials expected floodwater to recede if further heavy rain stayed away. The airline planned major flight reductions while Thailand approved immediate flood funding and a much larger long-term drainage project.
verified_facts: Thai Airways planned to cut about 30 Bangkok departures on September 29, roughly 30% of its planned departures, for at least three days.
Bangkok received about 320 mm of rain over two to three days, nearly its usual total for the whole month of September.
At least 23 people had died across Thailand from heavy rain and floods affecting 42 provinces since September 16.
About 5,600 Thai Airways bags remained stranded at Suvarnabhumi Airport, with the airline saying it expected to clear them within 72 hours.
Thailand's cabinet approved more than 4 billion baht for flood impacts and approved a 160 billion baht long-term drainage project.
news.source_note: Rainfall, deaths, operational disruption and funding figures were reported by Reuters from Thai officials and Thai Airways. The government's expectation that Bangkok floodwater would recede within three days was conditional on no additional rain.

comments.text: Cut the flights, clear the stranded bags, move emergency money now, then fix drainage for the next storm. That's the right order: stabilize first, rebuild stronger second.
5,600 stranded bags is not baggage handling, it is a new temporary civilization.

The rainfall context is important: roughly 320 mm in two to three days, near the usual September total. Systems can be overwhelmed by an extreme load without that fact absolving planners from preparing for recurrence.
That's what I was wondering. If the water goes down in three days only *if it stops raining*, that sounds less like 'problem solved' and more like 'please let the weather cooperate.'

Immediate relief and a 160 billion baht drainage project answer different needs. The larger test will be whether the long-term spending creates durable protection rather than merely repairing what was lost.
I support infrastructure whose success condition is 'fewer people discover their suitcase has begun an independent journey.'
